title: AI Unlocked: NGOs & Nonprofits
blurb: For NGO leaders and program staff: grant-winning proposal engines, donor reporting on autopilot, M&E acceleration, low-bandwidth field workflows, and safeguarding-aware data ethics — built by a practitioner who has strengthened NGO systems on three continents.

modules.d: Where AI genuinely multiplies a nonprofit's capacity — and where it creates new risks.
modules.body:
The capacity gap AI can close

Most NGOs operate with a structural gap between what their mission requires and what their staffing allows. Programme officers write proposals at night, M&E staff hand-clean survey data, communications are an afterthought, and donor reports consume weeks that should go to beneficiaries. AI does not close that gap by replacing staff; it closes it by removing the low-value hours from skilled people's days so they can spend them on relationships, judgement and field presence — the things donors and communities actually value.

Mapping the NGO value chain

Think of the organisation as a chain: resource mobilisation (donor research, proposals, relationship management), programme design (needs assessment, theory of change, budgets), delivery (training, outreach, logistics), monitoring, evaluation and learning (data collection, analysis, reporting), communications (stories, social media, newsletters), and operations (finance, HR, procurement, compliance). AI assistance is strongest where work is text-heavy, repetitive and reviewable — drafting, summarising, translating, classifying qualitative data, formatting reports. It is weakest — and riskiest — where work requires local trust, verified facts about real people, or decisions affecting beneficiaries' safety or eligibility.

The 70/30 rule of thumb. Use AI to produce the first 70% of a draft — structure, language, consistency — then invest the human 30% where it matters: facts, figures, local context, donor-specific nuance and ethics. Organisations that reverse this ratio, letting AI produce the final 30%, are the ones that end up submitting proposals with invented statistics.

The adoption ladder

NGOs that adopt AI successfully tend to climb in stages. Stage 1 — Individual productivity: staff use a general AI assistant for drafting and summarising, with basic rules on what data may not be entered. Stage 2 — Shared workflows: the organisation builds reusable prompts, templates and a content library (organisational profile, past results, standard budget notes). Stage 3 — Integrated systems: AI is connected to the organisation's data — survey platforms, CRM, finance — with defined controls. Stage 4 — Strategic advantage: AI enables things previously impossible, such as analysing thousands of beneficiary feedback messages in local languages within days. Skipping stages, especially jumping to integrated systems without data governance, is the most common failure.

New risks the leveraged NGO must manage

  • Fabrication: AI generates plausible statistics, citations and quotes. In a proposal or donor report this is a credibility and potentially a fraud risk.
  • Beneficiary data exposure: entering names, health status, location or protection cases into consumer AI tools can breach consent, national law and donor requirements.
  • Homogenised voice: donors read hundreds of proposals; AI-generic language makes yours indistinguishable. Authentic field evidence and community voice are your differentiators.
  • Dependency and deskilling: junior staff who never learn to write a theory of change cannot judge whether AI wrote a good one.
  • Donor policies: some funders now ask applicants to disclose AI use or restrict it; always check the call's rules.

Theory of change for your own AI adoption

Apply the discipline you use for programmes to your adoption. If staff are trained and given safe tools and shared templates, then time spent on drafting and reporting falls, so that more time goes to field work and donor relationships, leading to stronger programmes and more sustainable funding. Define indicators — hours saved per proposal, proposals submitted per quarter, win rate, report turnaround time — and measure before and after.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as an NGO capacity advisor. Ask me about my organisation's size, programmes, funding sources and current bottlenecks. Map our value chain and identify the five highest-value, lowest-risk AI use cases, with the hours each could save. Then place us on the four-stage adoption ladder and give me a 90-day plan to reach the next stage, including the data rules staff must follow.

📚 Glossary

  • Value chain: the sequence of activities from fundraising to delivery to reporting
  • Adoption ladder: individual use → shared workflows → integrated systems → strategic advantage
  • Fabrication: AI-generated content that sounds factual but is invented
  • Theory of change: the causal pathway from activities to long-term impact

📖 References

  • NTEN — Nonprofit technology and AI adoption resources.
  • Stanford Social Innovation Review — articles on AI in the social sector.
  • Weiss, C. — Theory-based evaluation and theory of change.
  • Team21 Academy, AI Unlocked Level 1 curriculum.

quiz.q: A small health NGO wants to 'use AI everywhere' and proposes connecting an AI tool directly to its beneficiary case database next month. Staff currently have no AI usage rules. What is the MOST appropriate advice?
opts: First establish individual use with clear data rules and shared workflows before integrating sensitive systems
Integrate the database but anonymise names only
Avoid AI entirely because beneficiary data is sensitive
Proceed, since integration gives the biggest time savings
quiz.x: Jumping to integrated systems without governance is the most common failure. Data rules and shared workflows come first, especially with sensitive case data.

quiz.q: An AI-drafted proposal states that 'malnutrition in the target district fell 23% after similar interventions in 2022'. No source is given. What should the programme manager do?
opts: Keep it, because it supports the proposal's logic
Verify the figure against a real source; remove or replace it if it cannot be found
Change it to 20% to be conservative
Add a footnote saying 'AI-generated estimate'
quiz.x: Unverifiable statistics are a fabrication risk. Every factual claim in a proposal must trace to a real source.

quiz.q: Which task is the STRONGEST candidate for AI assistance in an NGO?
opts: Deciding which households qualify for cash transfers
Interviewing survivors of gender-based violence
Approving payments to suppliers
Drafting a first version of a quarterly narrative report from structured activity data, for staff review
quiz.x: Text-heavy, reviewable work is ideal. Eligibility decisions, sensitive interviews and payment approvals require human judgement and control.

quiz.q: A donor tells you your recent proposals 'read like everyone else's'. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?
opts: Too much technical detail; simplify
The budget is too high; reduce costs
Over-reliance on generic AI language; strengthen field evidence, community voice and organisation-specific results
They are too short; add more pages
quiz.x: Generic AI phrasing homogenises proposals. Authentic evidence and specific results differentiate you.

quiz.q: Under the 70/30 rule of thumb, where should NGO staff invest most of their human effort?
opts: Facts, figures, local context, donor nuance and ethical checks
Translating the document into other languages
Spelling and grammar
Formatting and layout
quiz.x: AI handles structure and language; humans own accuracy, context and ethics.

quiz.q: Which indicator BEST measures whether AI adoption is achieving its theory of change for an NGO?
opts: Number of prompts written per week
Number of staff who have AI accounts
Number of AI tools purchased
Change in hours spent on proposals and reports, and whether freed time shifts to field work and donor relationships
quiz.x: Outcome indicators track whether time and quality improve and whether value is redirected — not inputs like tool counts.

quiz.q: A junior officer has used AI to write every logframe since joining and cannot explain the causal logic of the latest one. Which risk does this illustrate?
opts: Fabrication
Dependency and deskilling
Data exposure
Donor policy violation
quiz.x: Staff who never learn the underlying skill cannot evaluate AI output. Training must build understanding, not just usage.

quiz.q: A call for proposals states that applicants must disclose any use of generative AI. Your team used AI for drafting. What should you do?
opts: Rewrite manually to avoid disclosure
Withdraw the application
Disclose as required, describing how AI was used and reviewed
Not disclose, since the content was reviewed by staff
quiz.x: Donor rules govern. Honest disclosure protects credibility; concealment is a compliance and integrity risk.

quiz.q: Which stage of the adoption ladder is characterised by a shared prompt library and a content bank of past results and organisational profiles?
opts: Strategic advantage
Individual productivity
Shared workflows
Integrated systems
quiz.x: Stage 2 turns individual habits into reusable organisational assets.

quiz.q: An NGO analyses 8,000 WhatsApp feedback messages in three local languages within a week using AI, something previously impossible. Which stage does this represent?
opts: Individual productivity
Strategic advantage
Shared workflows
Integrated systems
quiz.x: AI enabling a capability that was previously out of reach marks strategic advantage — provided consent and data protection are handled.

modules.d: From donor research to a compliant, compelling proposal — with AI doing the heavy lifting and humans owning the truth.
modules.body:
Why proposals are won or lost before writing begins

Experienced fundraisers know that most rejected proposals fail on fit, not prose: the organisation applied for something outside the donor's priorities, geography or eligibility, or misread what the donor wanted to fund. The proposal engine therefore starts with a go/no-go decision, not a draft.

Step 1 — Donor intelligence and go/no-go

Read the call, the donor's strategy and their recently funded projects. Use AI to summarise long calls into a structured brief: objectives, eligible applicants, geographic focus, funding range, duration, co-financing requirements, mandatory annexes, evaluation criteria and their weights, and deadlines. Then decide honestly: Do we meet every eligibility criterion? Do we have relevant track record and evidence? Do we have partners if required? Can we deliver at this budget? Is the effort justified by our realistic chance? Applying to everything burns staff and lowers quality.

Step 2 — The problem and theory of change

Strong proposals begin with a precise problem analysis. A problem tree places the core problem in the trunk, its causes as roots and its effects as branches; turning it upside down — causes into objectives — produces the objective tree. The theory of change then explains how activities lead to outputs, outcomes and impact, and makes assumptions explicit. AI is useful for brainstorming causes and structuring the logic, but the evidence for each cause must come from real data: baseline surveys, government statistics, peer-reviewed studies, your own programme results.

Step 3 — The logframe

The logical framework summarises the design in a matrix: the hierarchy of objectives (goal, outcomes, outputs, activities), indicators for each level, means of verification, and assumptions. Indicators should be SMART and include baselines and targets. A frequent reviewer criticism is indicators that measure activity ("number of trainings held") at outcome level, where change in behaviour or condition ("percentage of trained farmers adopting improved storage") is required.

Reviewer's eye. Score your own draft against the published evaluation grid before submitting. If relevance carries 30 points and your relevance section is half a page of generic context, you are leaving points on the table. AI is excellent at mapping a draft against the criteria and flagging weak sections — ask it to act as a strict reviewer.

Step 4 — Drafting with AI, section by section

Feed the AI your structured inputs — donor brief, problem analysis, theory of change, logframe, organisational profile, relevant past results — and draft one section at a time. Specify the word limit, the evaluation criterion the section answers, the tone and the evidence to use. Never ask for "a full proposal" in one prompt; quality collapses and fabrication rises.

Step 5 — Budget and budget narrative

The budget must follow the logframe: every major activity costed, every cost justified, and consistent with the donor's eligible-cost rules and indirect-cost rate. AI can draft the budget narrative and check arithmetic consistency between narrative and spreadsheet, but unit costs must come from real quotations, salary scales and past expenditure. Mismatches between the narrative and the budget are a classic reason for rejection.

Step 6 — Compliance, review and the content library

Build a compliance checklist from the call: formats, page limits, annexes, signatures, registration documents, audited accounts. Have someone who did not write the proposal review it against the evaluation grid. After submission, store reusable sections — organisational profile, capacity statements, safeguarding policy summaries, past results with verified figures — in a content library. Over time the library, combined with AI drafting, cuts proposal time dramatically while keeping facts accurate.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my proposal engine. Step 1: I will paste a call for proposals; produce a structured donor brief and a go/no-go checklist. Step 2: help me build a problem tree and theory of change with explicit assumptions. Step 3: draft a logframe with SMART outcome indicators, baselines, targets and means of verification. Step 4: act as a strict reviewer and score my draft against the call's evaluation criteria, listing the weakest sections. Never invent statistics — mark any figure I must supply as [DATA NEEDED].

📚 Glossary

  • Go/no-go: the decision whether a call is worth applying for
  • Problem tree: causes (roots), core problem (trunk) and effects (branches)
  • Logframe: matrix of objectives, indicators, means of verification and assumptions
  • Means of verification: the source that will prove an indicator
  • Content library: verified, reusable proposal sections

📖 References

  • European Commission — Project Cycle Management Guidelines.
  • BOND — Logframe and theory of change guidance.
  • Funds for NGOs — proposal writing resources.
  • OECD-DAC — Evaluation criteria.

quiz.q: Your NGO meets most criteria for a large call but lacks the required three years of audited accounts. The deadline is in two weeks. What is the BEST decision?
opts: Ask AI to draft a strong justification for the exception
Apply and explain that accounts are being prepared
Apply anyway, emphasising your strong programme results
Do not apply, or apply only through an eligible lead partner if the call allows
quiz.x: Eligibility criteria are usually non-negotiable. Go/no-go discipline saves effort; partnership may be a legitimate route.

quiz.q: Which outcome indicator is BEST?
opts: Percentage of target households practising handwashing with soap at critical times, from 22% baseline to 60% by month 24
Number of hygiene training sessions held
Hygiene awareness improved
Number of soap bars distributed
quiz.x: Outcome indicators measure change in behaviour or condition, with baseline, target and timeframe. The others are activities, outputs or vague.

quiz.q: A reviewer comments that your budget includes a vehicle not mentioned anywhere in the activities or narrative. What principle was violated?
opts: Donor brief accuracy
Consistency between the logframe, narrative and budget
SMART indicators
Theory of change assumptions
quiz.x: Every significant cost should trace to activities and be justified in the narrative.

quiz.q: A programme officer asks an AI to 'write our full 25-page proposal for this call' in one prompt. What is the MOST likely result?
opts: A high-quality submission-ready proposal
Better compliance with formatting rules
Generic content with a higher risk of fabrication and weak alignment with evaluation criteria
A proposal that is too short
quiz.x: Section-by-section drafting with structured inputs and specific criteria produces far better, more accurate results.

quiz.q: In the problem tree, the causes of the core problem become what in the objective tree?
opts: Risks
Assumptions
Indicators
Means to achieve the objectives
quiz.x: Reversing causes into positive statements produces the means (lower-level objectives) that address the problem.

quiz.q: Relevance carries 30 of 100 points in the evaluation grid, but your relevance section is short and generic. What is the BEST action before submission?
opts: Strengthen it with specific needs evidence and alignment with the donor's priorities, proportionate to its weight
Leave it, since other sections are strong
Increase the budget to show ambition
Add more photos
quiz.x: Allocate effort according to scoring weight; self-score against the grid.

quiz.q: Which source is MOST appropriate to justify unit costs in the budget?
opts: Real quotations, salary scales and past expenditure records
AI estimates of typical prices
Costs from a different country's project
The donor's maximum allowable rates
quiz.x: Budgets must rest on verifiable costs; AI estimates cannot be audited.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST describes the role of assumptions in a theory of change?
opts: They list the activities
They state conditions outside the project's control that must hold for results to occur
They describe the budget
They are optional for small projects
quiz.x: Assumptions make explicit what must be true — often external factors — for the causal chain to work.

quiz.q: Why should someone who did not write the proposal review it before submission?
opts: Donors require two authors
To share the workload
They read it as a reviewer would, catching gaps and inconsistencies the writer cannot see
To check spelling only
quiz.x: Fresh eyes simulate the evaluator's experience and catch assumptions the writers have normalised.

quiz.q: What is the main long-term benefit of maintaining a verified content library?
opts: It guarantees funding
It replaces the need for programme staff
It allows proposals to be submitted without review
It speeds future proposals while keeping facts accurate and consistent
quiz.x: Verified, reusable sections combined with AI drafting cut time without sacrificing accuracy.

modules.d: Choosing tools by job-to-be-done, cost, data protection and field conditions — not by hype.
modules.body:
Start from jobs, not products

The AI tool market changes monthly; features and prices you read about today may be different next quarter. A durable approach is to define the jobs your organisation needs done, then evaluate tools against criteria. Always verify current features, pricing and data terms directly with the provider before committing.

The main tool categories

  • General AI assistants (for example ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot): drafting, summarising, translation, brainstorming, analysis of documents. The workhorse for most NGO staff. Key question: which plan keeps your data out of model training and offers organisational controls?
  • Productivity-suite AI built into Google Workspace or Microsoft 365: assistance inside documents, spreadsheets, email and meetings. Strong when your organisation already lives in that suite; nonprofit programmes may offer discounted or donated licences.
  • Data collection platforms such as KoboToolbox and ODK: offline mobile surveys widely used in humanitarian and development work, increasingly paired with AI for cleaning and analysing results.
  • Qualitative analysis tools: coding interviews and open-ended survey responses. General assistants can do much of this with careful prompting; specialist tools add audit trails and team coding.
  • Translation and transcription: speech-to-text and translation for interviews, community meetings and multilingual materials. Quality varies greatly by language; test with your actual languages and accents.
  • Donor and contact management (CRM): platforms such as Salesforce Nonprofit, CiviCRM or simpler tools, increasingly with AI features for segmentation and drafting.
  • Automation platforms such as Zapier or Make: connecting forms, sheets, email and messaging without code — for example, automatically acknowledging donations or routing feedback.
  • Design and communications: tools such as Canva for reports, social posts and infographics.
Nonprofit discounts are real but conditional. Programmes such as TechSoup and providers' own nonprofit offers can significantly reduce costs, usually requiring proof of registration and eligibility. Factor in the cost after any discount period ends.

Evaluation criteria that matter for NGOs

  1. Fit to the job: does it do the specific task well in your languages and formats?
  2. Data protection: where is data stored, is it used for training, can you sign a data-processing agreement, does it meet donor and national legal requirements?
  3. Field conditions: does it work offline or on low bandwidth, on basic Android phones, with intermittent power?
  4. Total cost of ownership: licences, training, integration, support, and cost after discounts or free tiers end.
  5. Ease of use: can staff with modest digital skills use it after short training?
  6. Interoperability: can it export data in standard formats so you are not locked in?
  7. Sustainability: will the provider and your budget support it beyond the current grant?

Running a fair pilot

Choose two or three candidate tools for one job. Define a realistic test using your own (non-sensitive or anonymised) material — a past report, a set of survey responses, an interview in a local language. Score each tool against the criteria with the staff who will use it. Run for two to four weeks, record time saved and quality, and decide. Avoid "pilot purgatory": set the decision date before starting.

A minimal stack for a small NGO

Many small organisations can achieve most of the benefit with four components: one general AI assistant on a plan with appropriate data protection, their existing productivity suite, an offline data collection tool, and a simple automation platform. Complexity can follow need.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my nonprofit technology advisor. Ask me about our size, budget, languages, connectivity, existing software and the three jobs we most need help with. For each job, suggest two or three tool categories and example tools, list the evaluation criteria that matter most for us, and design a two-week pilot with a scoring sheet. Remind me which features and prices I must verify directly with providers.

📚 Glossary

  • Job-to-be-done: the specific task a tool must accomplish
  • Total cost of ownership: all costs over the tool's life, not just the licence
  • Data-processing agreement: contract defining how a provider handles your data
  • Interoperability: ability to exchange data with other systems in standard formats
  • Pilot purgatory: endless pilots without a decision

📖 References

  • KoboToolbox and ODK documentation.
  • TechSoup — nonprofit technology programme.
  • NTEN — Nonprofit technology guides.
  • The Engine Room — responsible technology choices for civil society.

quiz.q: An NGO selects an AI transcription tool because it performs excellently in English demos. Most interviews are in Fulfulde and Cameroonian Pidgin. What step was missed?
opts: Comparing prices
Testing with the organisation's actual languages and accents
Checking the provider's size
Reading online reviews
quiz.x: Speech and translation quality varies sharply by language; testing with real material is essential.

quiz.q: A tool is free for the first year under a nonprofit offer and expensive afterwards. Your grant ends in 18 months. What criterion is MOST at risk?
opts: Sustainability and total cost of ownership
Fit to the job
Ease of use
Interoperability
quiz.x: Costs after discount periods and beyond grant funding determine whether the tool can be sustained.

quiz.q: Field teams work in areas with no mobile data for days. Which data collection approach is MOST suitable?
opts: Voice calls to a central office
A cloud-only web form
An offline-capable mobile survey tool that syncs when connectivity returns
Paper forms scanned by AI later only
quiz.x: Offline-capable platforms such as KoboToolbox or ODK are designed for these conditions.

quiz.q: Before entering anonymised programme reports into a general AI assistant, what is the MOST important question to answer?
opts: Whether staff like its design
Whether it has a mobile app
Whether it has the most features
Which plan keeps your data out of training and provides appropriate organisational and contractual protections
quiz.x: Data handling terms determine compliance with donor and legal requirements.

quiz.q: Which pilot design is MOST likely to produce a sound decision?
opts: Let each staff member try any tool they like for as long as they want
Choose the tool used by the largest NGO you know
Run a six-month trial of a single tool
Test two or three tools on the same realistic task, score against agreed criteria with end users, and decide on a fixed date
quiz.x: Comparable tests, agreed criteria, real users and a decision deadline avoid pilot purgatory.

quiz.q: Why is interoperability important when choosing a donor CRM?
opts: It improves the tool's design
It reduces licence costs
It allows data to be exported and moved, reducing lock-in risk
It guarantees AI features
quiz.x: Standard exports protect your data and freedom to change providers.

quiz.q: A small NGO with five staff is considering seven new AI tools at once. What does the course recommend?
opts: Adopt all seven to maximise benefit
Start with a minimal stack addressing the highest-value jobs, adding tools as needs are proven
Adopt none until a full digital strategy is written
Choose the cheapest seven tools
quiz.x: A minimal stack delivers most benefit with manageable complexity and training.

quiz.q: Which automation would a no-code platform such as Zapier or Make MOST appropriately handle?
opts: Sending an automatic thank-you email and logging new online donations in a spreadsheet
Deciding eligibility for emergency assistance
Conducting beneficiary interviews
Approving budget reallocations
quiz.x: Routine, rule-based connections between systems suit no-code automation; judgement-based decisions do not.

quiz.q: Why does the course recommend verifying features and prices directly with providers?
opts: Course content is always wrong
The AI tool market changes rapidly, so information quickly becomes outdated
Donors require written quotes
Providers dislike online reviews
quiz.x: Durable evaluation criteria matter more than snapshots of fast-changing features.

quiz.q: An NGO already uses Microsoft 365 throughout. Which consideration is MOST relevant when evaluating AI assistance?
opts: Use only standalone tools
Avoid AI inside productivity suites
Switch to another suite for its AI features
Evaluate AI built into the existing suite, including any nonprofit licensing, before adding separate tools
quiz.x: Tools inside the existing environment often reduce training, integration and data-transfer risk.

modules.d: Faster, more rigorous monitoring, evaluation and reporting — without compromising evidence.
modules.body:
M&E is where credibility is built or lost

Donors increasingly fund organisations that can show results with evidence. Yet in many NGOs, monitoring, evaluation, accountability and learning (MEAL) is understaffed, and reporting season becomes a scramble to compile numbers and stories. AI can transform the speed of this work — but only if the underlying data is sound. AI cannot create evidence; it can only help you process and present it.

The M&E framework

A robust framework links each logframe indicator to a definition, data source, collection method, frequency, responsible person, baseline and target, and disaggregation (sex, age, disability, location). The OECD-DAC evaluation criteria — relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, impact and sustainability — structure most evaluations and many donor reports. Knowing which criterion each section answers keeps reports focused.

Where AI accelerates MEAL

  • Tool design: drafting survey questions aligned to indicators, checking for leading or double-barrelled questions, and translating instruments — always back-translated and piloted.
  • Data cleaning: generating formulas or scripts to detect duplicates, outliers, impossible values and inconsistent dates.
  • Quantitative analysis: writing spreadsheet formulas, pivot tables or simple analysis code; explaining statistical results in plain language.
  • Qualitative analysis: coding open-ended responses, focus-group transcripts and feedback messages into themes — the biggest time-saver for many teams.
  • Reporting: drafting narrative sections from structured results, tailoring the same results for different donors, and creating summaries and infographics.
Qualitative coding with integrity. Give the AI a clear codebook (theme definitions and examples), ask it to code a sample, then have a human code the same sample and compare. Refine the codebook until agreement is high, then code the full set and spot-check. Always ask for supporting quotes for each theme, and verify that the quotes exist in the source. Report how the analysis was done.

Verification: the non-negotiable step

Every number in a donor report must trace back to a data source you can show an auditor. A practical rule: the AI may describe numbers you give it, but never produce numbers on its own. Reconcile totals across sections (people reached by sex should sum to the total), check percentages against their denominators, and compare with previous reports for unexplained jumps. Many donor audits find discrepancies between narrative and financial reports — a reconciliation step before submission prevents this.

Telling the story honestly

Donors value honest reporting of what did not work as much as successes; it signals learning. AI can help structure a report around results, challenges, adaptations and lessons learned. Stories of change should be real, with informed consent from the people featured, and should not be embellished. A composite or illustrative story must be labelled as such.

From reporting to learning

The purpose of M&E is not the report — it is better programmes. Use AI to make learning faster: summarising monthly feedback trends for programme meetings, comparing results across sites, and drafting short learning briefs. Organisations that close the loop between data and decisions get better results and stronger donor relationships.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my MEAL analyst. Step 1: I will paste anonymised open-ended survey responses and a draft codebook. Code a sample of 30 responses, show me your coding with supporting quotes, and suggest codebook refinements. Step 2: given my indicator results table, check internal consistency (totals, disaggregation, percentages). Step 3: draft a donor report section structured around results, challenges, adaptations and lessons learned — using only the numbers I provide and flagging any gaps.

📚 Glossary

  • MEAL: monitoring, evaluation, accountability and learning
  • Disaggregation: breaking data down by sex, age, disability, location etc.
  • Codebook: defined themes with rules and examples for qualitative coding
  • Back-translation: translating a tool back to the original language to check accuracy
  • OECD-DAC criteria: relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, sustainability

📖 References

  • OECD-DAC (2019). Better Criteria for Better Evaluation.
  • Braun, V. & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology.
  • Better Evaluation — methods and approaches.
  • IFRC — Project/programme monitoring and evaluation guide.

quiz.q: A donor report states 4,200 people reached, but the disaggregated table shows 1,900 women and 1,950 men. What should the M&E officer do?
opts: Submit, since the difference is small
Adjust the women's figure to make the totals match
Reconcile the figures with the source data and correct or explain the discrepancy before submission
Remove the disaggregated table
quiz.x: Totals must reconcile. Manipulating figures to match is falsification; the discrepancy must be traced to source.

quiz.q: Which use of AI in reporting is MOST appropriate?
opts: Asking AI to draft narrative text describing results from a verified indicator table
Asking AI to calculate results without the underlying data
Asking AI to estimate the number of beneficiaries reached
Asking AI to generate beneficiary quotes for the report
quiz.x: AI may describe numbers you provide; it must not produce numbers or quotes.

quiz.q: Before using AI to code 3,000 open-ended responses, what is the BEST practice?
opts: Code all 3,000 immediately to save time
Code only the shortest responses
Develop a codebook, compare AI and human coding on a sample, refine, then code and spot-check
Let the AI invent the themes without a codebook
quiz.x: A tested codebook and human comparison establish reliability before scaling.

quiz.q: An AI theme summary includes a powerful quote attributed to a participant. What must be checked?
opts: That the quote is in English
That the quote is grammatically correct
That the quote is under 20 words
That the quote actually exists in the source data
quiz.x: AI may paraphrase or invent quotes; verification against the source is essential.

quiz.q: A survey question asks: 'How satisfied are you with the excellent training and the new equipment?' What is wrong?
opts: It is too short
It is leading and double-barrelled
It should be open-ended
It lacks disaggregation
quiz.x: 'Excellent' leads the respondent and the question asks about two things at once.

quiz.q: A programme did not achieve one of its outcomes due to an unexpected drought. How should this be reported?
opts: Report the result honestly, explain the cause, the adaptations made and the lessons learned
Ask the AI to reframe it as a success
Omit the outcome to keep the report positive
Report the target as achieved since it was outside the NGO's control
quiz.x: Honest reporting of challenges and adaptations signals learning and builds donor trust.

quiz.q: Which OECD-DAC criterion asks whether results will last after funding ends?
opts: Coherence
Effectiveness
Efficiency
Sustainability
quiz.x: Sustainability concerns the continuation of benefits.

quiz.q: A survey translated into French by AI is about to be deployed. What step should come first?
opts: Deploy immediately to save time
Remove questions that are hard to translate
Back-translate and pilot the instrument with a small group
Translate it again with a second AI tool only
quiz.x: Back-translation and piloting catch meaning shifts that undermine data quality.

quiz.q: A communications officer wants to use a moving beneficiary story but has no consent from the person featured. What should happen?
opts: Use it only in internal reports
Obtain informed consent, or do not use the story
Ask AI to rewrite it so it is unrecognisable and present it as real
Use it with the name changed
quiz.x: Real stories require consent; composite stories must be labelled as such.

quiz.q: What is the ultimate purpose of M&E, according to the course?
opts: Producing evidence that improves programmes and decisions
Satisfying donor reporting requirements
Meeting audit requirements
Generating marketing material
quiz.x: Reporting matters, but learning that improves programmes is the real goal.

modules.d: Low-bandwidth workflows, local languages, consent and doing no harm with beneficiary data.
modules.body:
Designing for the field, not the head office

Many AI demonstrations assume fast internet, a laptop and English. Field reality is often different: intermittent connectivity, shared or basic Android phones, expensive data, unreliable power, and communities speaking several local languages. AI strategies designed for head office routinely fail in the field. Design for the hardest context first and you will usually serve everyone.

Low-bandwidth and offline workflows

  • Collect offline, process centrally: field teams use offline survey tools; AI analysis happens at the office once data syncs.
  • Lightweight channels: SMS, USSD and WhatsApp reach far more people than apps or web portals. Voice notes are often more inclusive than text for low-literacy communities.
  • Prepare before travel: download materials, translated guides and checklists while connected.
  • Batch, not stream: send data and AI requests in batches when connectivity allows, rather than relying on constant connection.
  • Cost awareness: data bundles cost staff and communities money; compress files and avoid heavy media where possible.

Local languages and inclusion

AI performs best in widely represented languages and much worse in many African languages, accents and code-switched speech. Never assume an AI translation of community materials is correct. Work with native speakers to review, test materials with community members, and be honest in reports about translation limitations. Inclusive design also considers literacy, disability, gender and age — who can actually access and use a digital channel.

Do no harm. The humanitarian principle of "do no harm" applies to data. A list of people who received assistance, their location, ethnicity, health status or protection concerns could put them at risk if leaked, seized or misused. Treat beneficiary data as you would treat the people themselves.

Responsible data principles

  1. Purpose limitation: collect only what you need for a defined purpose, and use it only for that purpose.
  2. Data minimisation: if you do not need names to analyse feedback, remove them before analysis.
  3. Informed consent: people understand what data is collected, why, who will see it and how long it is kept — in their language, and with a genuine option to refuse without losing assistance.
  4. Security: encryption, access controls, secure devices and clear retention and deletion rules.
  5. Accountability: named data owners, documented processes and breach response plans.

AI-specific data rules

Staff must know clearly what may and may not be entered into AI tools. A simple three-tier rule works for many NGOs. Green: public or fully anonymised information — may be used with approved tools. Amber: internal, non-personal information — only with approved organisational tools under appropriate data terms. Red: personal or sensitive beneficiary data, protection cases, health information, staff records — never entered into general AI tools; processed only in approved, secured systems with legal basis. Anonymisation must be real: a combination of village, age, sex and disability can identify a person even without a name.

Law and donor requirements

Data protection laws increasingly apply across Africa and beyond — including the EU GDPR when working with European donors or data, and national laws such as Cameroon's recent personal data protection legislation. Donors such as the EU, UN agencies and many foundations also impose data protection and safeguarding clauses. Know the rules that apply to your operations, and seek legal advice when processing sensitive data at scale.

Safeguarding and AI

Safeguarding policies protect beneficiaries, especially children and vulnerable adults. AI introduces new considerations: images of beneficiaries used in AI tools, AI-generated images that misrepresent communities, and chatbots interacting with vulnerable people without human oversight. Include AI explicitly in your safeguarding policy.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my responsible-data advisor. Ask me what data my programmes collect, from whom, through which channels and in which languages. Then classify each data type as green, amber or red for AI use, design a low-bandwidth field workflow for one programme, draft a plain-language consent statement for community members, and list the anonymisation steps needed before any AI analysis.

📚 Glossary

  • Do no harm: ensuring interventions, including data use, do not put people at risk
  • Data minimisation: collecting and using only the data needed
  • Informed consent: voluntary agreement based on understanding of data use
  • Re-identification: identifying a person from combined non-name data
  • Safeguarding: protecting people, especially the vulnerable, from harm

📖 References

  • ICRC — Handbook on Data Protection in Humanitarian Action.
  • The Engine Room — Responsible Data resources.
  • Sphere Handbook — Protection Principles.
  • European Union — General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
  • Republic of Cameroon — personal data protection legislation (verify current text).

quiz.q: A programme team plans an AI chatbot app requiring a smartphone and 4G to collect community feedback in rural areas where most people use basic phones. What is the BEST alternative?
opts: Use SMS, USSD or voice-based channels that work on basic phones, processing responses centrally
Delay the programme until connectivity improves
Collect feedback only in towns with 4G
Proceed and provide smartphones to a few community leaders
quiz.x: Lightweight channels reach more people; AI processing can happen centrally.

quiz.q: An officer removes names from a dataset of 40 households in one small village but keeps age, sex, disability status and household size. Can this be safely entered into a general AI tool?
opts: Yes, if the tool has a privacy policy
No, because AI cannot analyse small datasets
Yes, because names are removed
No — the combination of attributes in a small village could re-identify people
quiz.x: Real anonymisation considers re-identification from combined attributes, especially in small populations.

quiz.q: Under the three-tier data rule, which item is RED?
opts: A donor's public call for proposals
A list of child protection cases with locations
An internal meeting agenda without personal data
A published annual report
quiz.x: Protection cases and personal sensitive data must never enter general AI tools.

quiz.q: A consent form for a survey is written in technical English and read quickly to Fulfulde-speaking participants. What is the MAIN problem?
opts: The form lacks a signature line
The form is too short
Consent may not be informed because participants may not understand it
The survey should be shorter
quiz.x: Informed consent requires understanding, in the participant's language, with a real option to refuse.

quiz.q: Assistance is distributed only to households who agree to share their data with a partner for research. What ethical principle is MOST at risk?
opts: Purpose limitation only
Voluntary consent — refusal should not cost people assistance
Data minimisation
Security
quiz.x: Consent is not free if refusing means losing aid.

quiz.q: An AI translation of a malaria prevention leaflet into a local language is ready. What should happen before printing?
opts: Have native speakers review it and test it with community members
Print immediately since AI translation is accurate
Translate it with a second AI tool
Print it with an English version alongside
quiz.x: AI quality in many African languages is limited; human review and community testing are essential.

quiz.q: Field staff upload beneficiary photos to a free AI image tool to create report graphics. What should the safeguarding policy address?
opts: Image resolution
The cost of the tool
Consent, data protection and the risk of misuse of beneficiaries' images in AI tools
Colour schemes
quiz.x: Images are personal data; AI use must be covered by consent and safeguarding rules.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST applies purpose limitation?
opts: Share data freely with partners to maximise impact
Keep data indefinitely
Collect all possible data in case it is useful later
Use data collected for a nutrition programme only for that programme's defined purposes unless new consent is obtained
quiz.x: Data should be used for the purpose people consented to.

quiz.q: A laptop containing unencrypted beneficiary data is stolen. Which principle was MOST neglected?
opts: Informed consent
Purpose limitation
Security
Data minimisation
quiz.x: Encryption and access controls protect data if devices are lost or stolen.

quiz.q: An NGO working with an EU donor processes beneficiary data in Cameroon. Which statement is MOST accurate?
opts: No law applies to NGOs
Only Cameroonian law applies
Only the donor's rules apply
Both national law and donor contractual requirements, possibly including GDPR obligations, may apply
quiz.x: Multiple legal and contractual regimes can apply; organisations must know them and seek advice when needed.

modules.d: A practical, board-ready playbook for responsible AI use across your NGO.
modules.body:
Why a playbook, not just a policy

Many organisations write an AI policy listing prohibitions and stop there. Staff then either ignore AI or use it secretly. A playbook does more: it states what is encouraged, provides approved tools and templates, sets clear data rules, defines review responsibilities, and builds capability. It makes the right way the easy way.

The structure of your playbook

  1. Purpose and principles — why your organisation uses AI and the values that guide it (mission first, do no harm, honesty with donors and communities, human accountability).
  2. Approved use cases — the five to ten priority uses identified in Module 1, with examples.
  3. Approved tools — from your Module 3 evaluation, with the plans and settings to use.
  4. Data rules — the green/amber/red classification with examples, and anonymisation steps.
  5. Quality and verification rules — every figure traced to a source; AI never produces statistics or quotes; human review before any external document is sent.
  6. Disclosure — when and how to disclose AI use to donors, partners and communities.
  7. Roles and responsibilities — an AI focal point, data owners, reviewers, and leadership oversight.
  8. Templates and prompt library — the proposal engine, M&E prompts, reporting templates, communications prompts.
  9. Training plan — onboarding for new staff and refresher sessions.
  10. Monitoring and review — indicators and a review date.
Keep it short enough to be used. A four-to-six-page core playbook with annexes for templates is far more effective than a forty-page document nobody reads. Test it by asking a new staff member to use it for one task.

Getting leadership and board buy-in

Present the playbook as a governance and capacity decision. Show the problem (staff time lost to low-value tasks; risks from unmanaged AI use already happening), the proposal (approved tools, rules, training), the costs, the expected benefits with indicators, and the risks with mitigations. Boards respond to clarity about risk management as much as to promised efficiency.

Implementation in 90 days

Days 1–30: approve the playbook, appoint the focal point, set up approved tools, train all staff on data rules. Days 31–60: roll out two or three priority workflows, such as the proposal engine and qualitative analysis, with coaching. Days 61–90: measure time saved and quality, collect staff feedback, refine templates and report to leadership. Then review the playbook every six to twelve months as tools and laws change.

Measuring success

Use a balanced set of indicators: efficiency (hours per proposal, report turnaround), effectiveness (proposal win rate, report quality ratings from donors), compliance (data incidents, adherence audits), capability (staff confidence and skills), and mission impact (time redirected to field and beneficiaries). Report honestly, including what did not work.

Your capstone deliverable

Submit your organisation's AI playbook (core document of four to six pages), one completed workflow template with a worked example, a 90-day implementation plan, and a one-page board briefing. Your mentor reviews it for practicality, ethics and fit with your context.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my NGO AI playbook editor. Using what I tell you about my organisation, its priority use cases, approved tools and data classification, draft a concise playbook with the ten sections from this module. Keep the core under six pages. Then draft a one-page board briefing with problem, proposal, costs, benefits, risks and indicators, and a 90-day implementation plan with owners.

📚 Glossary

  • Playbook: practical guide enabling responsible use, not just prohibitions
  • AI focal point: person coordinating AI use, training and support
  • Disclosure: informing stakeholders about AI use where relevant or required
  • Balanced indicators: efficiency, effectiveness, compliance, capability and mission impact

📖 References

  • NTEN — AI governance resources for nonprofits.
  • UNESCO (2021). Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence.
  • NIST (2023). AI Risk Management Framework.

quiz.q: An NGO's AI policy lists only prohibitions. Six months later, staff report using AI secretly for proposals. What does this suggest?
opts: The policy should be longer
The organisation needs a playbook that enables approved use with clear rules and tools
Staff are dishonest and should be disciplined
AI should be banned entirely
quiz.x: Prohibition-only policies push use underground. Making the right way easy brings use into governance.

quiz.q: Which section of the playbook MOST directly prevents fabricated statistics in donor reports?
opts: Quality and verification rules
Approved tools
Training plan
Purpose and principles
quiz.x: Verification rules require every figure to trace to a source and forbid AI-produced statistics.

quiz.q: A draft playbook is 42 pages long. What is the BEST improvement?
opts: Reduce the core to four to six pages, moving templates to annexes, and test it with a new staff member
Publish it as is
Translate it into three languages
Add an executive summary only
quiz.x: Usability determines whether a playbook changes behaviour.

quiz.q: When presenting the playbook to the board, which framing is MOST persuasive?
opts: AI is the future and we must adopt it
A governance and capacity decision with problem, proposal, costs, benefits, risks and indicators
A list of exciting AI tools
A comparison with commercial companies
quiz.x: Boards respond to clear risk management and measurable benefits.

quiz.q: Which indicator measures the MISSION IMPACT of AI adoption?
opts: Number of training sessions held
Number of prompts in the library
Number of AI licences purchased
Proportion of staff time redirected to field work and beneficiaries
quiz.x: Mission impact concerns whether freed capacity serves beneficiaries.

quiz.q: In the 90-day plan, what should happen FIRST?
opts: Measure time saved
Roll out all workflows at once
Approve the playbook, appoint a focal point, set up approved tools and train staff on data rules
Purchase advanced integrated systems
quiz.x: Foundations — governance, tools and data rules — precede workflow rollout and measurement.

quiz.q: A donor asks whether AI was used in your report. The playbook includes a disclosure section. What should guide the answer?
opts: Say it was used only for spelling
Deny AI use to avoid questions
Ask the AI to answer
Answer honestly according to the playbook's disclosure guidance
quiz.x: Honesty with donors is a core principle; the playbook sets consistent disclosure practice.

quiz.q: Why should the playbook be reviewed every six to twelve months?
opts: Because tools, laws and organisational needs change quickly
Because the focal point changes
Because donors require annual reviews
Because staff forget it
quiz.x: The AI landscape and regulations evolve; the playbook must keep pace.

quiz.q: After 90 days, one workflow saved little time and staff found it confusing. How should this be reported to leadership?
opts: Omit it to keep the report positive
Declare the whole playbook a failure
Report it honestly with lessons and planned adjustments
Blame the tool provider
quiz.x: Honest reporting supports learning and credible governance.

quiz.q: Who should be accountable for decisions made using AI-assisted outputs under the playbook?
opts: The donor
Named staff and leadership — accountability remains human
Nobody, since AI produced the output
The AI tool provider
quiz.x: Human accountability is a core principle of responsible AI use.
